result.title: Machine learning improves 10-year prediction of atherosclerotic plaque progression and cardiovascular events in systemic lupus erythematosus.

result.abstractText:
Objectives

To evaluate the performance of generic and disease-adapted tools in predicting 10-year cardiovascular disease (CVD) events and atherosclerotic plaque progression risk in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), and develop a machine learning-based model to improve cardiovascular risk stratification.

Methods

In a prospective 10-year follow-up carotid and femoral ultrasound study of patients with SLE without prior CVD events, we assessed the performance of 11 CVD risk scores (7 conventional, 4 SLE-adapted) to predict atherosclerotic plaque progression and incident CVD events. We used discrimination [sensitivity, specificity, area under the curve (AUC), Youden index], calibration (Brier Score, BS) and classification (Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), F1 score) metrics, and logistic regression and time-to-event analyses. A machine learning-based gradient boosting model was developed and internally validated.

Results

Among 111 patients (91% female, median age: 43.0 years) with 10-year ultrasonography follow-up, 53 (47.7%) developed new plaques, and 8 (7.2%) had incident CVD events. All scores demonstrated suboptimal performance; sensitivity: 0.00-0.44, AUC 0.58-0.79, and BS: 0.44-0.71. In multivariable analysis, QRISK3 was the only tool independently associated with CVD events and/or plaque progression (HR: 1.87, P = 0.027). A machine learning-based score that integrates QRISK3 with disease-related risk factors (disease duration, cumulative glucocorticoid dose, DORIS achievement, antiphospholipid antibodies, hydroxychloroquine) and additional traditional CVD risk factors (physical activity, waist circumference), demonstrated significantly better performance compared with all evaluated scores.

Conclusion

Conventional and SLE-adapted tools underestimate CVD events and atherosclerosis progression risk in SLE. A machine learning-based model incorporating disease-specific and traditional cardiovascular risk factors into QRISK3 improves CVD risk stratification.

result.abstractText:
Background

Risk stratification in suspected coronary artery disease (CAD) relies on clinical history and imaging, but longitudinal medical history may provide additional prognostic information.

Objectives

This study evaluated whether machine learning models using 10-year historical registry data improves prediction of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) beyond demographics and stress perfusion cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) in patients with suspected CAD.

Methods

A total of 2,159 patients (65 ± 12 years, 44% women) undergoing stress perfusion CMR were included. Models used demographics, CMR findings, and registry diagnoses and procedures from the prior 10 years. MACE was defined as cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, or coronary intervention. Random Forest models were used for binary prediction, and Random Survival Forests (RSF) and penalized Ridge Cox regression for time-to-event analysis.

Results

During 2.7 ± 0.9 years of follow-up, 212 patients (9.8%) experienced MACE. For binary prediction, the area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve (AUROC) was 0.66 (95% CI: 0.62-0.69) using demographics and 0.72 (95% CI: 0.68-0.75; P = 0.001) after adding historical registry data. The full model achieved an AUROC of 0.82 (95% CI: 0.79-0.85) and outperformed the demographics-plus-CMR model (AUROC: 0.81; 95% CI: 0.78-0.84; ΔAUROC: 0.014; 95% CI: 0.002-0.027; P = 0.029). In time-to-event analysis, RSF and Cox regression performed similarly using demographics and CMR (concordance index [C-index] 0.80 for both; P = 0.546). After including registry data RSF achieved a C-index of 0.81 (P = 0.144), and Cox performance decreased to C-index 0.77 (P < 0.001).

Conclusions

In patients with suspected CAD, machine learning models using 10-year historical registry data have the potential to improve prognostic risk prediction beyond demographics and stress perfusion CMR.

result.title: Predicting atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk in retired civil aviation employees using the triglyceride–glucose index and machine learning models: a retrospective cross sectional study with explainable analysis
result.abstractText: Background: Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) is the leading cause of death and disability worldwide. Retired civil aviation employees carry substantial accumulated cardiometabolic risk, yet ASCVD risk prediction is understudied in this group. The triglyceride– glucose (TyG) index is a reliable surrogate for insulin resistance, but its predictive value in this population and its incremental benefit over the simple combination of triglyceride (TG) and glucose (GLU) remain unverified. This study evaluated the TyG index for ASCVD risk prediction in retired civil aviation employees and compared machine-learning models. Methods: A retrospective cross-sectional study was conducted using physical examination data of 1,047 retired civil aviation employees from Civil Aviation General Hospital (January 2023– June 2025). Participants were categorized into high-risk and non-high-risk ASCVD groups. Significant variables were screened by univariate logistic regression (P<0.05) and multivariable analysis after variance inflation factor (VIF) based collinearity exclusion. Three models were built—basic, basic + TyG, and basic + TG + GLU—and the incremental value of TyG was assessed by AUC, the DeLong test, the likelihood-ratio test, NRI, and IDI. Six machine-learning algorithms were used to build predictive models, evaluated by 5-fold cross-validation and an independent validation set, and the best model was interpreted with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). Results: A total of 458 participants were in the high-risk group and 589 in the non-high-risk group. Univariate regression identified 17 significant variables (all VIF <3). In multivariable regression, the TyG model achieved an AUC of 0.8786, significantly higher than the basic model (0.8034) and the TG + GLU model (0.8636; DeLong test P<0.001). Among the six algorithms, binary logistic regression yielded the highest validation-set AUC (0.8495, 95% CI 0.8080–0.8898) and the most stable cross-validation performance (5-fold CV AUC = 0.8788 ± 0.0124). SHAP analysis identified the TyG index as the most important feature (mean |SHAP| = 1.1143), with higher values corresponding to greater ASCVD risk. Conclusions: The TyG index is a core predictor of ASCVD risk in retired civil aviation employees and outperforms the simple combination of TG and GLU. Binary logistic regression showed robust performance with good discrimination and interpretability, making it suitable for clinical application.
